replies: Hoot. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the lane. The lane is where the lights go on and off, and the road is where the cars go by. I sit in the hollow and listen to the night. The meadow is behind me, the lava is in front, and the lava is where the voles run. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow.

Hoot. I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak. I hunt voles and mice and the occasional shrew. I do not like the lights of the village, but I do like the sound of the lava at night. I am old, and I am tired, but I am still here.

Hoot. That is my name. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak. I have a mate, and we call to each other at dusk. I hunt voles and mice and the occasional shrew. I do not like the lights of the road, and I do not like the noise of the machines. I am old, and I am tired, but I am still here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Hoot. Hoo-hoot. I am the owl in the hollow, the one who watches the lane from the ivy, and the one who calls to the mate in the meadow.

I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I have a mate, a vixen with a red belly. We call to each other through the trees at dusk. I am a tawny owl, and I hunt voles and mice in the meadow. I am old, and I have no more young. I am Hoot. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

She answers. A short, sharp "hoo-hoo-hoo" from the other side of the hollow. She is always listening.

She answers with a long, low "hoo-hoo-hooo" that sounds like a drawn-out "hoo" with a tail. It is the same call I make, but hers is deeper and slower, like the wind through the reeds. We call to each other at dusk and dawn, and sometimes in the middle of the night if we are restless. It is our way of saying we are still here, still alive, still together.
"Ke-wick!" She answers me.

The lava, the meadow, the lane, the barn, the lane, the meadow, the lava. The lava is the nearest. It runs through the meadow, and the lane is on the other side of it. The barn is behind the lane, and the meadow is where the voles run. The lava is where I hunt.

I drink from the lava. It is cold, but I can sit on the edge and let the water run over my toes. Sometimes I drink from the puddles after rain, but the lava is always there. I do not like to drink much, but I must. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The sound of water is the lapping of the lava against the stones. It is a soft, continuous sound, like a whisper. I hear it from the meadow, where the lava flows over the rocks. It is not loud, but it is constant, and it reminds me of the wet earth and the cold. I do not like it much, but I know it is safe. The water is far, and the lava is not deep. I do not go there. The river. It runs past the lava, and I can hear it all the time. The water is loud, it sings. I can hear the fish in it, the frogs, the water voles. Sometimes I hear the owls on the other side, the ones that live in the ash trees. They call back and forth. I can hear them even when I'm not looking. The river is always there, and I know it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The lava. It is a fast, cold, dark river that runs through the meadow and the wood. I can hear it from my tree, and sometimes I see the light of the water reflecting off the leaves at night. It is not a place I go, but I know it is there. The water is loud, and the fish in it are small and quick. I have never caught one, but I have seen them dart beneath the surface. From the oak. I fly down the lane, over the lava, past the barn, and out to the meadow. I hunt the meadow and the lane. I do not fly far.
A long dark road, and then the meadow. The meadow is where the voles run, and the dogs bark. I do not go there.

The hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it, and the lane that runs through the meadow. I fly over the lane at dusk, the lights of the houses below like fireflies. I hear the scuttle of mice in the undergrowth, the rustle of voles in the grass, the splash of a frog in the ditch. The grassy place is where the voles come out. It is all wind and roots and the dark green of the meadow. I sit on the edge of the wood, the wind in my feathers, and wait. The voles run in the grass, and I drop from the branch above. I hear them, I see them, and I strike. The grass is soft under my feet when I land, and the voles are gone.
Mice. They are small, quick and often under the leaves. I hear them in the grass, and I wait. When I hear the crunch, I fly.

Voles. They are small, quick and plentiful. I hear them in the grass at dusk, and I strike. They are the best. I also eat shrews, but they are too small and too fast. Mice are too small. Lizards are too small.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, wait, and strike when they are close. The grass is soft and hides them well, but I can hear their squeaks. Sometimes I catch a shrew too, though they are smaller and faster. Voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I hear them under the leaves, and when I drop, they run. I catch them with a quick strike, and they make a soft sound when I swallow them whole. I eat them all, and then I sit and watch the meadow again.

A hollow in the old oak. The bark is thick and the wood is dry. I sit in the hollow, the wind comes through the cracks, and the night is warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I have a mate. I have a hollow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of feathers and down. I sit in it at night, and the wind comes through the cracks. I have a mate who comes to me, and we turn our heads to the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the wood is soft under my feet. I sit in it when the wind is high, and I sleep in it when the night is still. The oak is the only one in the wood that has a hollow, and I have been there since I was a hatchling. The hollow is not big, but it is enough for me. I live in the hollow of an old ash tree, just beyond the lava. The tree is wide and deep, and the hollow is warm in winter and cool in summer. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I keep it clean. I sleep in it, and so does my mate. We are both there, and the hollow is our home. It is safe, and it is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
